problem: The reflect/transmit roles are swapped. In an optical see-through combiner the real light is transmitted through the mirror and the virtual light from the microdisplay is reflected off it, so each loses part of its light on its own path. As written ('reflects part of the real light and transmits part of the virtual light') the sentence is physically backwards and contradicts Section 1, which a student may memorise as fact.
fix: Brightness: the combiner transmits only part of the real light and reflects only part of the virtual light, so both images arrive dimmer than they left the source.

problem: 'The computer image is focused into the eye by a combiner' gives the focusing job to the combiner. A combiner is a mirror or waveguide; it overlays, it does not focus. The focusing/collimation is done by the lens optics in front of the microdisplay.
fix: The computer image is collimated by the display optics and reflected into the eye by a combiner, while real light passes straight through that same combiner.

problem: 'The eye sits a few centimetres behind and below the optics' overstates the distance. Eye relief on a beam-splitter or waveguide display is typically about 15–25 mm, i.e. one to two and a half centimetres, and this number matters when students size the eyebox.
fix: Eye offset: the eye sits about 15–25 mm behind the optics (the eye relief) and slightly below the optical axis, so the virtual image is drawn from a point that is not the eye centre...

problem: The caption says monitor-based AR is the fourth case shown, but the tree has only three children (Optical, Video, Projection). A student reading the figure will look for a branch that is not there.
fix: Either add a fourth 'Monitor-based (screen, no eyewear)' node to the tree, or change the caption to say monitor-based AR is the fourth arrangement described in the text and is not drawn.

problem: This paragraph is placed inside the projection/choosing section, but it is a property of head-worn fixed-focus displays, not of projection (a projected image lies on the real surface, so accommodation and vergence agree). Sitting where it does, it reads as if it applies to all four routes.
fix: Move the paragraph to the end of Section 2 (or Section 3) and open it with 'In any head-worn fixed-focus display, including both see-through types, ...'; add one line that projection AR does not suffer from it because the image is focused on the real surface.

where: Section 2, 'No occlusion' bullet and Quiz Q3
problem: 'A virtual object cannot hide a real one' and Q3's 'never hide' are stated absolutely, but the Beyond box then describes switchable liquid-crystal shutters and per-pixel dimming that do block real light exactly where the virtual object is drawn. The two statements sit badly together.
fix: Qualify both: 'In a plain combiner design a virtual object cannot hide a real one ...' and in Q3 'Why can a basic optical see-through display not hide a real object behind a virtual one?'
